title: Nicodemus by night (John 3:1–8)
hookLine: born again of water and the Spirit; the Church hears baptism here
carry: the wind bloweth where it will

cards: Some questions only come out at night. At two in the morning, a person asks what they couldn't ask at lunch. Today a man comes to Jesus with that kind of question, and John tells us he came by night.
His name is Nicodemus: a Pharisee, a respected teacher, a ruler among his people, a serious student of the scriptures. He has seen the signs, and he's honest about it.
Rabbi, we know you are a teacher come from God; nobody could do these signs unless God were with him. And Jesus answers a question he hasn't asked yet.

teach.b: Jesus says: "Amen, amen I say to thee, unless a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word translated again, anothen, can also mean from above.
Born again, born from above; John seems to want both. Nicodemus takes it literally and asks the almost comic question: can a grown man go back into his mother's womb?
Jesus goes further: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." This is where the Catholic Church hears baptism.

The Catechism calls baptism a new birth by water and the Spirit and points to this very verse. Since the earliest centuries, Christians coming up out of the font have been called newly born. Then a picture.
In Greek, pneuma means both wind and spirit.
The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, reads it as Spirit: "The Spirit breatheth where he will; and thou hearest his voice, but thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth."
Many other English Bibles, the King James among them, read it as wind, blowing wherever it will, and today's line holds that reading. Both are faithful to the Greek.
You can't see the wind or steer it; you hear it in the trees and see what it moves. Nicodemus, the careful scholar, is told this new birth is not something he can schedule.
And John will bring him back twice, the last time carrying a hundred pounds of spices to the tomb.

how: The Catholic Church reads John 3:5 as speaking of baptism, the new birth by water and the Spirit, and this passage is often read at baptisms and in the Easter season.

o: a teacher who comes by night

p: a Pharisee who came by night

s: he came honestly: rabbi, we know you are a teacher come from God.
in Greek, wind and spirit are the same word
pneuma. the Douay reads Spirit, the King James reads wind.
he returns twice in John, the last time bringing spices for Jesus's burial.

games.q: you're Nicodemus. this teacher has just told you a man must be born again. you're a grown man and a scholar. what do you ask?
o: how can a man be born when he is old?
games.why: he takes it literally and asks how a man can enter his mother's womb again. Jesus answers: of water and the Spirit.

practice: Let a question come that you usually keep for the dark, about God, yourself, someone you love, what happens after, and don't answer it; just let it be asked, the way Nicodemus asked his. You're allowed to ask it.
If you pray, bring it to God as it is; if you don't, just hold it honestly.

wordCard.voice: Anothen. The Greek word meaning both again and from above, at the heart of Jesus' answer to Nicodemus in the dark. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: again, anew, and also from above (John 3:3). Both senses seem meant.

carryVoice: Your line: the wind bloweth where it will. And that's week seventy-one: great joy, logos, the Word made flesh, Agnus Dei, the fig tree, the first sign, and Nicodemus.
